svg.text: How a request is handled
The applicant writes in plain English. The app checks the law, then either answers with numbers or opens a locked room for the records.
1 The request
Who is asking
What they want to do
Which numbers or records
JSON or the web form
2 Law check (AI + law text)
What will the results be used for?
The AI picks the matching rule out of
the regulation and quotes it verbatim.
Records only if the applicant explains
why statistics are not enough.
Art. 54 · 53 · 66 of Regulation (EU) 2025/327
REJECTED — prohibited use (Art. 54)
e.g. an insurer that wants to raise premiums for people with diabetes.
The applicant sees the rule that forbids it, quoted from the law.
APPROVED — anonymised statistics (Art. 53, 69)
The plain-English definitions are translated into a database query —
nothing is written by hand per request. Rules first, AI only as a fallback.
Small groups are hidden: counts under 10 show as “<10”, a percentage or
mean on fewer than 10 people is “suppressed”. Opted-out patients never count.
APPROVED — records in a secure room (Art. 66, 68, 73)
Only the selected patients and only the record types asked for are copied
into a separate environment, opened with a one-day access key.
Inside: browse and query. Results appear only as watermarked images.
Download is always refused (403) and every attempt is logged.
What never leaves the app
• Patient data stays in one local database. The AI (Claude via OpenRouter)
only ever sees the request text and the law text — never a patient record.
• The AI never decides alone: it chooses from rules we retrieved and must
quote them; if the quote is not in the law text, staff review the case.
• Numbers are computed by code, not by the AI, so they are the same every run.
• Patients who opted out are excluded from every answer and every room.
• A flooding client is blocked for a minute (rate limit per address).
20,000 synthetic patients from three Austrian hospitals · no real data
